plain: There are many ways to keep your house cool in summer without cranking the AC nonstop. Close blinds or curtains during the hottest parts of the day to block direct sunlight, especially on south- and west-facing windows. Use ceiling or box fans to circulate air, since moving air feels several degrees cooler even without lowering the temperature. Run heat-generating appliances like ovens and dryers in the early morning or evening instead of midday. Open windows at night when outdoor air is cooler, then seal the house up in the morning to trap that cooler air inside. Reflective window film or blackout curtains can significantly reduce heat gain. Planting shade trees outside sun-facing windows blocks heat before it even enters. Finally, a programmable thermostat set slightly higher when you're away saves energy while keeping things comfortable when you're home.

plain: We, the Be IRL movement, declare that presence is a right worth reclaiming. Every day, our attention is pulled from the people beside us into screens designed to hold it hostage. We believe a conversation deserves your full face, not a glance stolen between notifications. We believe a sunset is not improved by being photographed, and a meal tastes better without being filmed first. We commit to leaving our phones in our pockets or bags during meals, walks, and gatherings with others. We commit to noticing our surroundings: the weather, a stranger's kindness, the texture of an ordinary afternoon. We reject the idea that being constantly reachable makes us more connected; often it makes us less present to the one thing that matters most, the people and world actually in front of us. Be here. Be real. Be IRL.

plain: How long you need to work before retiring depends heavily on your income, savings rate, expected expenses in retirement, and when you want to stop working, so there's no single universal answer. A common rule of thumb, the 4% rule, suggests you need roughly 25 times your expected annual expenses saved to retire comfortably. Someone who saves aggressively, say 30-50% of their income starting in their 20s, might be able to retire in their 40s or 50s, a path often called financial independence or FIRE. Someone saving a more typical 10-15% might work until traditional retirement age, around 65 to 67 in the U.S., when Social Security benefits also become available. Employer-matched retirement accounts, pensions, and Social Security all factor into the calculation, so it's worth working with a financial planner to estimate your own timeline.
